lesson.title: Mapping the Internet: A Mesh, Not a Hierarchy
lesson.summary: The internet's topology is a loose, decentralized structure of interconnected autonomous systems, running from small access networks up through regional providers to a handful of global backbones, held together by bilateral agreements rather than central design.
lesson.body:
Zoom out from the mechanics of any single protocol and ask what the internet actually looks like as a shape, and the honest answer is that it is not a single tidy structure. It is a rich, evolved mesh of autonomous systems connected however their operators have found it useful and profitable to connect them. It helps, though, to have a rough mental model, because most of those connections do follow recognizable patterns even if the overall picture resists being drawn as a clean diagram.

At one end sit access networks and end networks, the ones that connect actual users, homes, offices, campuses, and individual servers, to the rest of the internet. These typically do not have a rich mesh of their own connections, they buy connectivity from someone larger. In the middle and toward the core sit progressively larger regional and national networks, which connect many smaller access networks together and, in turn, connect upward or outward to still larger networks to reach destinations they do not serve directly. At the very top of this loose structure sit the largest global backbone networks, covered next as tier 1 networks, which between them are interconnected richly enough that no destination on the internet requires paying anyone above them for reachability.

The important caveat is that this description is a loose hierarchy, not a strict one, and it is really more of a convenient mental picture than an architectural rule. Networks at similar levels frequently connect directly to each other sideways, bypassing the layer above them entirely, when doing so is mutually useful, and a single autonomous system can simultaneously play different roles toward different neighbors, buying transit from one network while peering as an equal with another and selling transit to a third. This is a direct consequence of the fact that every one of those connections is really just a bilateral BGP relationship between two autonomous systems, shaped by whatever business terms the two operators agreed to. There is no central authority drawing the overall diagram or enforcing a hierarchy on it. The internet's topology today is the accumulated, decentralized result of many individual, independently negotiated agreements, which is also exactly why it has proven so resilient: there is no single choke point whose failure disconnects the whole structure, traffic can generally find an alternate path through the mesh.
